title: Rabin-Karp — Rolling Hash

title: Rabin-Karp — Rolling Hash
text:
How Rabin-Karp Works
The Rabin-Karp algorithm uses hashing to speed up string matching. Instead of comparing every character at every alignment, it computes a hash fingerprint of the pattern and of each length-m window of the text. If the hashes differ, the window cannot match — skip it without any character comparisons.
Key ideas:

Hash-based filtering. Compute h(P) once. At each shift s, compute h(T[s..s+m-1]) and compare it to h(P). Only when the hashes agree do we verify character-by-character.
Rolling hash. Re-computing the hash from scratch at every position would be just as slow as naive matching. A rolling (incremental) hash lets us update the window hash in O(1) using the formula h_new = (d * (h_old - T[s] * d^(m-1)) + T[s+m]) mod q.
Spurious hits. Two different strings can hash to the same value (a collision). When hashes match but the strings differ we call it a spurious hit. The algorithm is still correct because every hash match is verified, but spurious hits add extra work.

The polynomial rolling hash used here is:
\[h(s) = \bigl(s_0 \cdot d^{m-1} + s_1 \cdot d^{m-2} + \cdots + s_{m-1}\bigr) \bmod q\]
with alphabet size d = 256 and a small prime q = 101 (chosen small so you can follow the arithmetic by hand).

title: Rabin-Karp — Rolling Hash
text:
Hash Function Visualization
Step through each window position. The top row shows the text with the current window highlighted. Below it, the hash of the window is compared to the hash of the pattern. On a hash match the algorithm verifies character by character — a real match turns green, a spurious hit turns yellow. The progress bar at the bottom summarizes all positions.









viewof T_rk = Inputs.text({label: "T:", value: "abcaabcabcaab", width: 400})
viewof P_rk = Inputs.text({label: "P:", value: "abcab", width: 400})
viewof d_rk = Inputs.range([2, 256], {step: 1, value: 256, label: "d (alphabet size):"})
viewof q_rk = Inputs.range([2, 997], {step: 1, value: 101, label: "q (prime modulus):"})






































viewof step_rk = Inputs.range([0, rk_max_step], {step: 1, value: 0, label: "Step:"})

title: Rabin-Karp — Rolling Hash
text:
Rolling Hash Step-by-Step
This visualization shows how the rolling hash is updated from one window to the next. At each step:

The outgoing character T[s] (red) is removed by subtracting T[s] * d^(m-1).
The running value is multiplied by d (the base shift).
The incoming character T[s+m] (green) is added.
The result is taken mod q.










viewof T_roll = Inputs.text({label: "T:", value: "abcaabcabcaab", width: 400})
viewof P_roll = Inputs.text({label: "P:", value: "abcab", width: 400})
viewof d_roll = Inputs.range([2, 256], {step: 1, value: 256, label: "d (alphabet size):"})
viewof q_roll = Inputs.range([2, 997], {step: 1, value: 101, label: "q (prime modulus):"})






































viewof step_roll = Inputs.range([0, roll_max_step], {step: 1, value: 0, label: "Step:"})

title: Rabin-Karp — Rolling Hash
text:
Comparison with Naive
How many character comparisons does Rabin-Karp need versus naive matching? When the hash function distributes well (few spurious hits), Rabin-Karp verifies only at real matches — vastly fewer character comparisons than the naive approach which must compare at every position.
Try lowering q to a very small prime (e.g. 2 or 3) to see how more collisions increase the character comparison count.

Naive String Matching
Step through every single character comparison. At each shift s, the algorithm compares P[0] vs T[s], then P[1] vs T[s+1], and so on. On a mismatch it backtracks to the next shift and starts over from P[0] — this is the repeated work that makes the naive approach slow.

title: Keyword Tree — Multiple Pattern Matching
Keyword Tree — Multiple Pattern Matching
text:
Aho-Corasick: Failure Links & Output Links
The keyword tree alone restarts from the root at every position. The Aho-Corasick automaton adds two types of pointers:

Failure links (red dashed): when the descent gets stuck, jump to the longest proper suffix of the current path that is also a prefix of some pattern.
Output links (green dotted): chain together all patterns that end along the failure-link path, so patterns ending at internal nodes are not missed.

  label: "Patterns (comma-separated):",
  value: "he, she, his, hers",
  width: 500
})

title: Ukkonen’s Algorithm — Online Suffix Tree Construction
text:
Phase-by-Phase Suffix Tree Construction
Ukkonen’s algorithm builds the suffix tree online, one character at a time. Each phase processes one character and extends all active suffixes. Use the slider to step through the phases and watch the tree grow.
Remember to include a unique end marker (like $) so every suffix ends at a leaf.
Three extension rules govern what happens at each step:

Rule 1 (leaf extension): the suffix already ends at a leaf — the leaf grows automatically (implicit, via global end).
Rule 2 (new branch): the suffix ends at a point with no continuation for the new character — split the edge and create a new leaf.
Rule 3 (already exists): the new character is already present — do nothing and stop the phase (showstopper).


viewof S_uk = Inputs.text({label: "S:", value: "cacao$", width: 300})















viewof phase_uk = Inputs.range([0, uk_max_phase], {step: 1, value: 0, label: "Phase:"})

title: Ukkonen’s Algorithm — Online Suffix Tree Construction
text:
Suffix Links Visualization
Suffix links are the key to Ukkonen’s O(n) complexity. If an internal node represents string ax (where a is a single character and x is a possibly empty string), its suffix link points to the node representing x.
This view shows all suffix links in the final suffix tree. Suffix links allow the algorithm to jump from one extension to the next in O(1) amortized time, instead of restarting from the root.
